- Medora (historic downtown): Chateau de Mores State Historic Site, the Cowboy Hall of Fame, shops and restaurants — an easy complement to a South Unit visit. ([medorand.org](https://medorand.org/things-to-do?utm_source=openai))  
- Painted Canyon Visitor Center & Overlook: a dramatic first/last stop right on I‑94 with great views and interpretive info before you enter the South Unit. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Short park hikes & scenic drives to add: Wind Canyon, Coal Vein, Buck Hill and the Park’s scenic loop drives are all high‑value, short options for wildlife and badlands panoramas. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Elkhorn Ranch site (Roosevelt’s “home ranch”): a separate, very remote unit about ~35 miles north of Medora; gravel roads lead there and it’s an easy ~0.75‑mile walk from the parking area to the cabin foundations. Plan for gravel driving and limited services. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/national-park/elkhorn-ranch?utm_source=openai))  
- Maah Daah Hey Trail & rough‑country riding/hiking: a long, scenic non‑motorized single‑track (100+ miles) that connects with areas near the park — great for day hikes or mountain‑biking outside the park. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/nearbyattractions.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Bully Pulpit Golf Course and family attractions in Medora (mini‑golf, zipline, amphitheatre events): nice non‑hiking options if you want a slower day. (Many events — e.g., the Medora Musical — are seasonal in summer.) ([medora.com](https://medora.com/attractions-activities/?utm_source=openai))  
- Rough Rider State Park / trailheads: good for camping, trail access, and linking into Maah Daah Hey route. ([parkrec.nd.gov](https://www.parkrec.nd.gov/sites/www/files/documents/Stay/2026%20State%20Parks%20Guide-WEB.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
- Practical note: Dickinson (~35 miles east) is the nearest larger town with groceries, restaurants and medical services. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))

Great question — Medora is small but stuffed with Badlands scenery, history, and uniquely Western experiences. Here are the best things to do, with quick notes and practical tips:

Top things to do
- Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit): drive the 36-mile scenic loop for superb badlands views and wildlife (bison, prairie dogs, wild horses); short hikes (Painted Canyon, Ridgeline, Petrified Forest) depart from the loop. Check road/status at the visitor center before you go. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/drive-the-south-unit-scenic-drive.htm?utm_source=openai))

- See the Medora Musical at the Burning Hills Amphitheatre: the long-running outdoor variety show is Medora’s signature night activity (seasonal summer run). Book tickets early for summer dates. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/))

- Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library: a major, immersive museum just outside town (opened in 2026). Plan several hours for exhibits + the boardwalk and views. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/?utm_source=openai))

- Bully Pulpit Golf Course: an 18‑hole course set in the Badlands — highly scenic and popular, so reserve tee times in advance. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/bullypulpit/?utm_source=openai))

- Pitchfork Steak Fondue: Medora’s theatrical, cowboy‑style dinner experience — fun dinner option (seasonal; often bundled with show packages). ([medora.com](https://medora.com/pitchforksteakfondue/))

- Maah Daah Hey Trail & Point-to-Point Trails: world‑class singletrack for mountain biking, long-distance hiking, and horseback access; also short town‑adjacent trails if you don’t have time for the full trail. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/do/?utm_source=openai))

- Horseback trail rides and wagon rides: guided rides from Medora Riding Stables let you see the badlands from the saddle; wagon rides give a short historic town tour. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/trailrides/?utm_source=openai))

- Point to Point Park (family fun): mini‑golf, Manitou Zipline, lazy river/ pool, splash pad and illusion house — good for families or a break from hiking. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/pointtopoint/?utm_source=openai))

- Chateau de Mores & North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame: historic house museum about Medora’s founder (the Marquis de Mores) and a small museum celebrating western/ranching heritage. Good indoor options and short tours. ([history.nd.gov](https://history.nd.gov/historicsites/chateau/?utm_source=openai))

- Scenic overlooks & Painted Canyon Visitor Center (I‑94 exit): a quick stop if you’re arriving on the interstate — great first views of the badlands and a short nature trail. ([medorand.org](https://medorand.org/things-to-do?utm_source=openai))

Practical tips
- Best time: summer (June–September) is peak activity season — the Musical, many tours, and Point-to-Point are seasonal. The TR Presidential Library and the national park are accessible year‑round but some services are seasonal. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/))  
- Reserve ahead: Medora Musical shows, Pitchfork Steak Fondue dinners, Bully Pulpit tee times, and guided trail/horse rides can sell out — book early for summer weekends. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/))  
- Wildlife & safety: stay in/near your vehicle for close wildlife sightings (especially bison), carry water, sunscreen, and layers — Badlands weather can change quickly. Check NPS alerts and trail status before hiking. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/things2do.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- How long to stay: 1–2 full days will cover the South Unit scenic drive, a short hike or trail ride, and one evening show; add a day if you want to play golf, bike the Maah Daah Hey segments, or spend more time at the TR Library. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/drive-the-south-unit-scenic-drive.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Where to eat/stay: Medora has a handful of seasonal restaurants, a few small hotels and unique stays (conestoga wagons, historic inns); town lodging fills fast in summer. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/))

Want a brief sample itinerary?
- Day 1: Arrive → Painted Canyon overlook → South Unit scenic drive + short hikes → dinner in town.  
- Day 2: TR Presidential Library in the morning → horseback or Point-to-Point Park in afternoon → Medora Musical + (optional) Pitchfork Fondue dinner. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/hiking-and-trail-information.htm?utm_source=openai))

If you tell me when you plan to go (dates or time of year) and whether you prefer hiking, history, family activities, or adventure (zipline/golf/horseback), I can suggest a tailored 1–3 day itinerary and booking priorities.

Great — I can do a custom 3‑day plan. Quick question before I finalize: where will you start/end (Bismarck, Dickinson, Williston, or another town)? And what are your priorities — hiking/photography/wildlife, history & museums, or a relaxed scenic drive with short walks? If you don’t have a preference, below is a ready-to-go sample 3‑day loop based out of Dickinson that hits western North Dakota’s top must-sees.

Sample 3‑day itinerary (start/end Dickinson, ND)

Day 1 — Medora & Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit)
- Morning: Drive Dickinson → Medora (about 35–40 miles, ~35–40 min). Pick up maps/tips in Medora. ([flattestroute.com](https://www.flattestroute.com/Medora-to-Dickinson-ND?utm_source=openai))  
- Midday: Painted Canyon Visitor Center, South Unit scenic loop drive (stop at Buck Hill, Wind Canyon overlooks, Maltese Cross cabin). Plan 3–4 hours for driving + short walks and wildlife viewing. The South Unit is the park’s most visited unit and Medora is the gateway town. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Evening: Explore Medora (historic de Mores Chateau, town square). If you’re visiting in summer, consider the Medora Musical (seasonal, nightly in summer) — buy tickets early. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/?utm_source=openai))

Day 2 — North Unit & Watford City
- Morning: Drive Medora → Theodore Roosevelt NP North Unit / Watford City (North and South units are distinct; expect ~1–1.5 hours between units depending on route). Head to the North Unit entrance and take the 14‑mile scenic drive with numerous pullouts (Cannonball Concretions, River Bend, Oxbow Overlook). ([peacegardenalmanac.com](https://peacegardenalmanac.com/stories/theodore-roosevelt-national-park-north-vs-south-unit?utm_source=openai))  
- Afternoon: Short hikes (Little Mo Nature Trail, Caprock Coulee options) and wildlife watching (bison, prairie dogs, feral horses). Stay overnight in Watford City (services and lodging there). Allow a half–full day (3–6 hours) inside the North Unit if you like hiking and photo stops. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/park-brochure-formats.htm?utm_source=openai))

Day 3 — Enchanted Highway + Dickinson museums (return to Dickinson)
- Morning: Drive Watford City → Dickinson (~85–90 miles, ~1.25–1.5 hours). Continue to Regent and drive the Enchanted Highway — 32 miles of giant scrap‑metal sculptures with pullouts and picnic spots; the route is free and open any time. Allow 1–2 hours to stop at most sculptures and photos. ([rome2rio.com](https://www.rome2rio.com/s/Watford-City/Dickinson-ND-USA?utm_source=openai))  
- Afternoon: Back in Dickinson visit the Dickinson Museum Center / Badlands Dinosaur Museum (great for regional history and fossils) before wrapping up. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/dickinson/attractions-entertainment/educational-attractions/dickinson-museum-center?utm_source=openai))

Must‑see stops (short list)
- Theodore Roosevelt National Park — South Unit (Painted Canyon, Maltese Cross Cabin) and North Unit scenic drive/overlooks. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library (new major attraction at Medora — opened 2026) — strongly worth a stop if you’re in Medora. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/?utm_source=openai))  
- Enchanted Highway — 32 miles of giant steel sculptures outside Regent (free, always open). ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/itineraries/enchanted-highway?utm_source=openai))  
- Maah Daah Hey Trail & Little Missouri Badlands — famous single‑track for hiking/biking (144 miles total; if you want a day hike, pick a short section). ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/maah-daah-hey-trail?utm_source=openai))  
- Dickinson Museum Center / Badlands Dinosaur Museum — good regional museum and fossils. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/dickinson/attractions-entertainment/educational-attractions/dickinson-museum-center?utm_source=openai))  
- Knife River Indian Villages NHS (if your route includes Bismarck): excellent for Indigenous and Lewis & Clark history (near Stanton). ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/knri/planyourvisit/basicinfo.htm?utm_source=openai))

Practical tips and logistics
- Fuel/cell: services are thin in the Badlands — top off gas and download offline maps before long stretches. Medora and Dickinson are the most reliable service points. ([medorand.org](https://medorand.org/getting-here?utm_source=openai))  
- Park fees & payment: Theodore Roosevelt NP charges an entrance fee (vehicle and per‑person options) and moved to cashless payments on May 1, 2026 — bring a card or digital payment. Reserve campsites on Recreation.gov if camping. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/learn/news/theodore-roosevelt-national-park-to-move-to-cashless-fee-collection-starting-may-1.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Wildlife safety: maintain safe distances (use binoculars/long lens); NPS guidance typically advises staying about 25 yards from bison and other large animals — don’t approach or feed wildlife. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/idkt_lnt6.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Timing/season: summer (Memorial Day–Labor Day) is peak for Medora events and many visitor services; shoulder seasons are quieter and can be beautiful (fall colors), but check hours. The Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library opened July 4, 2026 and is now a key draw in Medora. ([cavmir.com](https://cavmir.com/locations/medora-north-dakota?utm_source=openai))  
- Gear: good walking shoes, sun protection, water (carry more than you think), binoculars or zoom lens for wildlife, and a small first‑aid kit.

Great route — there are a lot of memorable detours between Mount Rushmore (Keystone/Black Hills) and Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Medora area). Below are the best stops grouped by area, with one-line why-to-stop notes and a citation you can use to plan further. Quick note: a direct drive from Mount Rushmore to Medora is commonly quoted at about 4½ hours, so these are detours you add depending on time and interest. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/a-map-to-medora/?utm_source=openai))

Near Mount Rushmore / inside the Black Hills
- Custer State Park — Needles Highway, Sylvan Lake and abundant wildlife (bison/jackrabbits) make this a classic short-to-half‑day stop for scenic drives and short hikes. ([gfp.sd.gov](https://gfp.sd.gov/userdocs/docs/tatanka_2021.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
- Iron Mountain Road / Scenic viewpoints — the twisting scenic route (with pigtail bridges and carved tunnels) gives great views back toward Mount Rushmore. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rushmore?utm_source=openai))  
- Crazy Horse Memorial — large, ongoing monument project and museum complex a short drive from Rushmore. ([crazyhorsememorial.org](https://crazyhorsememorial.org/plan-your-visit/getting-to-crazy-horse-memorial?utm_source=openai))

Northern Black Hills / through the north route
- Spearfish Canyon Scenic Byway — spectacular canyon road with waterfalls (Roughlock Falls), great if you like a relaxed, scenic drive and short walks. ([recreation.gov](https://www.recreation.gov/camping/gateways/13857?utm_source=openai))  
- Deadwood — historic gold‑rush town with restored 19th‑century main street, museums, and Old West history if you want a cultural/historical stop. ([deadwood.com](https://www.deadwood.com/businesses/attractions/?utm_source=openai))

Iconic detour (a little out of the way, but popular)
- Devils Tower National Monument (Wyoming) — striking monolith and America’s first national monument — an excellent photo/hike stop if you want a notable natural landmark. (It’s a detour west from the Black Hills area.) ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/deto/planyourvisit/basicinfo.htm?utm_source=openai))

If you take the more easterly route (I‑90 corridor) or want Badlands scenery
- Wall Drug and Badlands National Park — classic roadside Americana (Wall Drug) and dramatically eroded badlands landscapes if you want stark prairie/badlands vistas. These lie east of the Black Hills and pair well together if you have extra hours. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Drug?utm_source=openai))

Approaching / at Theodore Roosevelt NP and Medora
- Theodore Roosevelt NP (South Unit, Medora) — the South Unit has a ~48‑mile scenic loop, river overlooks, and ranger programs; Medora itself has a historic Main Street, visitor services, and seasonal events. The Maah Daah Hey trail and Little Missouri grasslands around Medora are great for short hikes and scenic side-roads. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))

Quick planning tips
- Decide which “unit” of TRNP you’re heading to — most visitors go to the South Unit via Medora (visitor center and the main scenic drive). ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- Factor time for detours: Custer/Needles + Crazy Horse/Deadwood can be done in a day if you start early; Devils Tower is a longer out‑and‑back detour; Badlands + Wall can add several hours but are very rewarding. ([gfp.sd.gov](https://gfp.sd.gov/userdocs/docs/tatanka_2021.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Want this tailored to your trip?
- How many days / hours do you have for the drive?  
- Are you going to the South Unit (Medora) or the North/other unit of TRNP?  
- Driving an RV/camper or a car?

Nice question — I-94 across North Dakota is a surprisingly rewarding drive. Below are the best stops (west → east) with a short note on why each is worth pulling off for and the I‑94 exit or location to look for.

- Medora / Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit) — gateway to the Painted Canyon overlooks, short rim hikes, abundant badlands scenery, the Medora Musical and the new Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library area. Excellent for sunset photos and a real “Badlands” experience. (Exits ~24–32). ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/directions.htm?utm_source=openai))

- Enchanted Highway (Gladstone → Regent) — a 32‑mile string of giant scrap‑metal sculptures (Grasshoppers, Deer, Tin Family, etc.). Great quirky photo stop and very family‑friendly; begins at I‑94 Exit 72 (Gladstone). ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/regent/attractions-entertainment/family-fun/enchanted-highway?utm_source=openai))

- Dickinson / Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson Museum Center) — hands‑on dinosaur and regional history exhibits; good place for a break and an indoor stop especially if traveling with kids. (I‑94 Exit ~61). ([dickinsongov.com](https://www.dickinsongov.com/museum-center/page/visit-us?utm_source=openai))

- Salem Sue (New Salem) — the “World’s Largest Holstein Cow” perched on School Hill (visible from I‑94). Quick photo stop and short hill drive for panoramic prairie views (Exit 127 / New Salem). ([roadsideamerica.com](https://www.roadsideamerica.com/tip/2788?utm_source=openai))

- Bismarck / Mandan area — North Dakota Heritage Center & State Museum (state history), Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park (Custer house, reconstructed Mandan earthlodges), Dakota Zoo and riverboat cruises on the Missouri — a great mid‑state city stop with museums and restaurants (I‑94 Exit 157–161 area). ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/?utm_source=openai))

- Jamestown — National Buffalo Museum / North American Bison Discovery Center plus the large “Dakota Thunder” buffalo sculpture; an easy, family‑friendly stop not far off I‑94. ([discoverjamestownnd.com](https://discoverjamestownnd.com/fun-things-to-do-in-jamestown-nd/all-things-buffalo/worlds-largest-buffalo-monument/?utm_source=openai))

- Steele — “Sandy,” the World’s Largest Sandhill Crane (about 40 ft tall) just off I‑94 (Exit ~200). Quick photo/opportunity to stretch legs. ([maps.roadtrippers.com](https://maps.roadtrippers.com/us/steele-nd/points-of-interest/worlds-largest-sandhill-crane?utm_source=openai))

- Valley City / Sheyenne River Valley — notable Hi‑Line Railroad (rail) bridge views, the Sheyenne River Valley Scenic Byway (if you want a detour), and local museums — pretty river scenery and good cafés. (I‑94 Exits ~290–294 / Valley City). ([nsbfoundation.com](https://nsbfoundation.com/nb/sheyenne-river-valley-national-scenic-byway/?utm_source=openai))

- Fargo / West Fargo (east end of I‑94 in ND) — best for restaurants, museums and nightlife: Plains Art Museum, Fargo Theatre, Bonanzaville and the Red River Zoo are all close to I‑94. Good place for a last‑big stop or overnight. ([fargomoorhead.org](https://www.fargomoorhead.org/things-to-do/downtown-fargo/?utm_source=openai))

Practical / travel‑useful stops
- Painted Canyon Visitor Center / rest area in TRNP (east of Medora) is an especially scenic rest area with trails and overlooks. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))  
- North Dakota has multiple rest areas and welcome stations spaced along I‑94 (Beach welcome at the west entrance, Oriska rest area east of Valley City, etc.); check real‑time road/closure info with NDDOT before you go. ([dot.nd.gov](https://www.dot.nd.gov/news/new-oriska-rest-area-offers-expanded-amenities-travelers?utm_source=openai))

Want this turned into a printable/phone map or a 1‑day vs. multi‑day suggested itinerary (with driving times and how long to spend at each stop)? If yes, tell me your direction (west→east or east→west), how many hours or days you have, and what you like (nature, museums, quirky roadside stops, kid activities, restaurants).

Great question — the North Dakota Badlands (centered on Medora and Theodore Roosevelt National Park) are excellent for families. Quick list of kid-tested ideas with where to go and tips:

Top kid-friendly things to do
- Theodore Roosevelt National Park — scenic drives, wildlife viewing (bison, prairie dogs, wild horses) and easy, short trails plus a Junior Ranger program for kids. Great for short hikes and picture stops. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/hiking-and-trail-information.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Short, easy hikes good for kids — Wind Canyon Trail (≈0.4 mi, ~20 minutes) and Painted Canyon overlook/trail are short, dramatic and family-friendly. Perfect for little legs and big views. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/hiking-and-trail-information.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Medora town family attractions — Medora Children’s Park, Point to Point Park (mini golf, lazy river, zipline options), wagon/carriage rides and seasonal family shows. A handy base with kid activities within walking distance. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/activities?utm_source=openai))
- Maah Daah Hey Trail — pick short, easy sections for family hikes or beginner mountain-biking; the trail system has many multi-use segments suitable for kids when you choose a short, easy stretch. ([mdhta.com](https://mdhta.com/about/?utm_source=openai))
- Enchanted Highway — a free 32‑mile roadside art drive of giant metal sculptures with pullouts and picnic spots — a fun photo scavenger-hunt for kids. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/regent/attractions-entertainment/family-fun/enchanted-highway?utm_source=openai))
- Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson) & local fossil events — big mounted dinosaur displays are great for younger dino fans; the North Dakota Geological Survey and museums sometimes run family fossil digs or half‑day programs (check age restrictions). ([visitdickinson.com](https://www.visitdickinson.com/dino?trk=public_post-text&utm_source=openai))
- Guided floats/kayaks on the Little Missouri River — family-friendly guided trips are available (operators offer tandem options and age/skill guidance). Great for a calmer, watery way to see the badlands. ([littlewilderness.co](https://www.littlewilderness.co/new-events-2/north-dakota-float-trip?utm_source=openai))
- Horseback or wagon rides — guided trail rides and short wagon tours around Medora let kids experience the landscape like Roosevelt did (many stables have minimum age limits—check ahead). ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/activities?utm_source=openai))
- Camping & stargazing — cottonwood campgrounds and dispersed sites give big-sky nights for constellation spotting and easy campfire programs; bring warm layers and binoculars. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/npgallery/GetAsset/257b1284-d776-43d5-9a8f-863023a2e520?utm_source=openai))

Quick safety & planning tips
- Wildlife safety: always observe wildlife from a distance and never approach bison, horses or other large animals — view from the car or designated overlooks. Bring binoculars. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/dena/planyourvisit/wildlife-safety.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Bring lots of water, sun protection and closed-toe shoes (the sun and wind can be intense; trails are often exposed).
- Check seasonal hours and availability (many Medora attractions and guided activities are seasonal or have limited schedules). Call ahead for rides, kayak trips, museum hours, and fossil-program signups. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/activities?utm_source=openai))
- Trail difficulty varies — choose short official trails (Wind Canyon, Painted Canyon, Coal Vein) for younger kids; Maah Daah Hey sections can be rugged unless you pick an easy segment. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/hiking-and-trail-information.htm?utm_source=openai))

If you want, tell me:
- the kids’ ages and how many days you have, and whether you’ll be based in Medora — I can make a 1‑ or 2‑day family itinerary (with timed suggestions, food stops, and age-appropriate activity lengths).

Short answer: Theodore “T.R.” Roosevelt (1858–1919; president 1901–1909) transformed the presidency and the federal government — as a progressive reformer, trust-buster, energetic international actor, and the single most influential early‑20th‑century conservationist in U.S. history. Below are his major accomplishments, his conservation work in detail, and the main elements of his legacy (including important caveats).

1) Major accomplishments (political, economic, and foreign policy)
- Became the youngest U.S. president (assumed office Sept. 14, 1901) after President William McKinley’s assassination; elected in his own right in 1904.
- “Square Deal” domestic program: promoted consumer protection, corporate regulation, and labor rights as a balance between big business, labor, and public interest.
- Trust‑busting and regulation: prosecuted large monopolies (notably Northern Securities Company), enforced the Sherman Antitrust Act more aggressively, and strengthened federal regulatory power (e.g., expanded Interstate Commerce Commission authority).
- Consumer protection laws (1906): championed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act, prompted by public exposés like Upton Sinclair’s work.
- Labor policy: intervened as a neutral arbiter in the 1902 anthracite coal strike, securing a negotiated settlement and establishing a precedent for federal mediation.
- Strengthened the executive branch and presidency’s public role — used persuasion, investigations, and regulatory power to shape policy.
- Foreign policy and global posture: articulated “speak softly and carry a big stick,” expanded the U.S. Navy, backed construction of the Panama Canal (helping secure the 1903 treaty with the new Republic of Panama), and sent the Great White Fleet (1907–1909) to project American power.
- Nobel Peace Prize (1906): awarded for mediating the Russo‑Japanese War—he was the first American to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
- Party politics: his progressive turn split the Republican Party; in 1912 he ran as the Bull Moose/Progressive Party candidate, which helped elect Woodrow Wilson.

2) Conservation work (scope, institutions, and concrete actions)
- Philosophical shift: made conservation a national priority — argued that natural resources should be managed scientifically and preserved for public use and future generations.
- Institutional achievements:
  - Established the U.S. Forest Service (1905) and empowered professional forest management under Gifford Pinchot.
  - Signed the Antiquities Act (1906), giving presidents authority to designate national monuments to protect significant natural, cultural, or scientific features.
- Land protection and designations: during his administration he set aside vast areas of public land for conservation — commonly summarized as roughly 200–250 million acres (commonly cited figure: about 230 million acres) — by creating and expanding national forests, wildlife refuges, national parks, and national monuments.
  - Created and expanded many national forests (often reported as around 150 forest units), wildlife refuges (including numerous bird reserves), several national parks, and about a dozen–two dozen national monuments under the Antiquities Act.
- Legacy in conservation practice: promoted scientific management, professional forestry, game and wildlife protection, and a federal role in stewardship — a practical foundation for later conservation policy and agencies (e.g., the National Park Service, established 1916).

3) Legacy — lasting effects and controversies
- The modern presidency: greatly expanded executive authority, activist use of executive offices, and the idea that the president acts as a national moral leader for reform.
- Progressive reform and regulatory state: helped legitimize federal regulation of business, consumer protection, and government mediation of labor disputes — a forerunner of later progressive and New Deal reforms.
- Conservation and environmental policy: widely credited with creating the conservation movement’s institutional base in the U.S.; many of today’s public lands and conservation practices trace to his administration.
- Foreign policy and American power: made the U.S. a hemispheric and global power—Panama Canal, naval expansion, and the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) to the Monroe Doctrine shaped U.S. behavior in Latin America and abroad for decades.
- Political consequences: his 1912 third‑party run split Republicans and contributed to Democratic wins; his style pushed the Republican Party toward progressive reform and later conservative reactions.
- Complex record on race and civil rights: mixed and often criticized. He made notable gestures (e.g., inviting Black leader Booker T. Washington to the White House in 1901), but he also made decisions that upheld segregationist policies and failed to challenge systemic racism in many ways. This complexity is central to modern reassessments of his reputation.
- Personal and cultural imprint: an energetic, larger‑than‑life public figure — Rough Rider war hero image, outdoorsman, writer, and model of vigorous citizenship — that shaped American self‑image in the 20th century.

Short concluding assessment
Roosevelt reshaped American government and public life: he expanded federal power to regulate corporations and protect consumers, established the U.S. as an emerging world power, and created a durable federal conservation program that preserved enormous tracts of land and set management precedents still in use. His record is widely admired for progressive reform and conservation but is also critiqued for imperialistic foreign‑policy impulses and an uneven record on race.

Short answer: Theodore Roosevelt’s “Square Deal” was his domestic program (roughly 1901–1909) that aimed to ensure fairness for ordinary Americans by reining in concentrated corporate power, protecting consumers, and conserving natural resources. Its slogan was essentially “a square deal for every man,” and the policy rested on three main pillars often summarized as the “three Cs”: control of corporations, consumer protection, and conservation.

Details and examples

1) Control of corporations (trust regulation)
- Goal: Limit abuses of big business and make corporations answerable to the public while preserving efficient firms that behaved responsibly.
- Actions: More vigorous enforcement of the Sherman Antitrust Act (e.g., the Northern Securities antitrust suit that forced the breakup of a major railroad monopoly); laws targeting railroad abuses such as the Elkins Act (1903) against rebate practices and the Hepburn Act (1906) which strengthened the Interstate Commerce Commission’s regulatory power.

2) Consumer protection
- Goal: Protect public health and ensure truthful information about food and drugs.
- Actions: Pushed and signed major consumer-safety laws in 1906 — the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act — that increased federal oversight of food and pharmaceuticals and created standards for safety and labeling.

3) Conservation of natural resources
- Goal: Preserve natural resources and manage public lands scientifically for long-term public benefit rather than short-term private exploitation.
- Actions: Created or expanded national forests and parks, established professional forest management (U.S. Forest Service under Gifford Pinchot), supported the Newlands Reclamation Act (1902) for irrigation and western land development, and used the Antiquities Act to proclaim national monuments. (Roosevelt placed large tracts of public land under federal protection.)

Other important elements
- Labor mediation: Roosevelt intervened directly in the 1902 anthracite coal strike, urging arbitration and using the prestige and power of the presidency to secure a settlement — a new role for the federal government as neutral arbiter between labor and capital.
- Philosophy: He distinguished “good trusts” from “bad trusts” and argued the federal government should regulate rather than simply destroy corporations when necessary to protect the public interest.

Limitations and legacy
- The Square Deal advanced progressive reform and expanded the federal government’s regulatory and conservation roles — it helped define modern expectations of government responsibility for fairness, safety, and stewardship.  
- Limits: Roosevelt did not push far on redistributive income policy or on civil rights for African Americans, and some critics saw his approach as paternalistic or inconsistent (he regulated some industries while accommodating others).

Theodore Roosevelt was the 26th President of the United States. He served from September 14, 1901 (he succeeded William McKinley after McKinley’s death) until March 4, 1909 (after winning election in 1904 and serving one full elected term).

Major milestones of his administration

- Square Deal (domestic policy framework): stressed fairness for labor, consumers and business and supported progressive reforms to curb corporate power and protect the public.
- Trust-busting and regulation: aggressively enforced the Sherman Antitrust Act (notably the Northern Securities suit), and backed stronger federal regulation of big business.
- Railroad and commerce regulation: strengthened the Interstate Commerce Commission’s powers (Elkins Act, Hepburn Act) to curb unfair railroad practices.
- Consumer protection and public health: championed and signed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act (both 1906), prompted by public concern over food safety.
- Labor intervention: intervened in the 1902 anthracite coal strike, pressuring owners to negotiate and establishing the precedent of presidential mediation in major labor disputes.
- Conservation and natural resources: greatly expanded federal conservation efforts — created the U.S. Forest Service (under Gifford Pinchot), established many national forests, bird reservations and national monuments (using the Antiquities Act of 1906), and set aside large tracts of public land for conservation.

Because Theodore Roosevelt National Park is split into three main areas—the **South Unit** (near Medora), the **North Unit** (near Watford City), and the remote **Elkhorn Ranch Unit**—there is a wide variety of historical, scenic, and roadside attractions scattered nearby. 

Depending on how far you want to drive, the top places to explore include:

---

### 1. In & Around Medora (South Unit Gateway)
If you base yourself in Medora, you don't have to drive far to find great attractions:
* **Château de Mòres State Historic Site:** The preserved 26-room summer home of the French aristocrat Marquis de Mòres, who founded Medora in 1883 and attempted to pioneer a refrigerated beef-packing empire. The site also includes the ruins of his meatpacking plant.
* **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame:** A high-quality museum detailing the Native American, ranching, and rodeo history of the northern Plains.
* **The Medora Musical & Pitchfork Steak Fondue (Summer only):** Held in the open-air Burning Hills Amphitheatre overlooking the badlands, this long-running Western revue is North Dakota's flagship summer attraction. Paired with steaks cooked on pitchforks over open vats of oil, it’s a classic Western experience.
* **Harold Schafer Heritage Center:** Free museum dedicated to the local businessman and philanthropist who restored and saved the historic town of Medora in the 1960s.

---

### 2. For Outdoor Enthusiasts
* **Maah Daah Hey Trail:** A legendary 144-mile singletrack trail running through the Little Missouri National Grassland, connecting the South Unit and the North Unit of TRNP. It is world-renowned among mountain bikers, long-distance hikers, and horseback riders. Even doing a short day hike along an access point offers deep solitude.
* **Little Missouri State Park:** Located about an hour north of Medora (and southeast of Watford City), this park is often called an "equestrian's paradise." It features 45 miles of trails winding through some of the most dramatic, razor-sharp badlands topography in the state.

---

### 3. Quirky & Fun Road Trips (Within 1 to 1.5 Hours)
* **The Enchanted Highway (Regent/Gladstone, ND):**
  * *Distance:* ~45 minutes east of Medora off I-94.
  * A 32-mile stretch of two-lane highway featuring giant scrap-metal folk-art sculptures, including *Geese in Flight* (recognized by Guinness World Records as the world's largest scrap-metal sculpture), *Deer Crossing*, and *Grasshoppers in the Field*. It ends in the tiny town of Regent, home to a whimsical gift shop and castle-themed hotel.
* **Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson, ND):**
  * *Distance:* ~35 minutes east of Medora.
  * Part of the Dickinson Museum Center, this is arguably the best dinosaur museum in the state. It holds the largest collection of real dinosaur fossils on display in the Dakotas, including a near-complete *T. rex* skull and fossilized skin impressions.
* **Makoshika State Park (Glendive, MT):**
  * *Distance:* ~1 hour west across the Montana state line on I-94.
  * Montana’s largest state park boasts otherworldly badlands, caprocks, and deep coulees rich in Hell Creek Formation dinosaur fossils. It features an excellent visitor center, paleontology displays, and a 5.5-mile scenic drive.

---

### 4. Historic Sites Worth the Detour (1.5 to 2 Hours)
* **Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site (near Williston, ND):**
  * Located roughly 1.5 hours north of the TRNP North Unit, right on the Montana border.
  * This was the most important fur-trading post on the upper Missouri River from 1828 to 1867. The fort has been meticulously reconstructed to its 1851 appearance and sits just above the confluence of the Missouri and Yellowstone rivers.
* **Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site (Stanton, ND):**
  * Located about 1.5 hours east of TRNP South Unit.
  * Preserves the remnants of major earth-lodge villages inhabited by the Mandan and Hidatsa peoples for centuries. It was here that Lewis and Clark met Sakakawea and Charbonneau in the winter of 1804–1805. You can tour a full-scale reconstructed earth lodge and walk among visible circular depressions where lodges once stood.

---

### Pro-Tip for Your Itinerary:
Make sure you **visit both units of Theodore Roosevelt National Park** itself. Many visitors only see the popular South Unit near Medora and skip the **North Unit** near Watford City (about 70 miles north). The North Unit features deeper canyons, greener valleys, dramatic overlooks like **Oxbow Overlook**, and a distinct, quieter vibe with large bison herds and bighorn sheep.

**Medora, North Dakota**, is a charming, historic Old West town nestled right at the entrance of the Badlands. While small, it punches far above its weight in attractions—especially from late spring through early autumn. 

Here are the best things to do when visiting Medora:

---

### 1. Explore Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit)
Medora serves as the gateway to the South Unit of this stunning, rugged park where Theodore Roosevelt once ranched.
* **Scenic Loop Drive:** Take the 36-mile scenic drive to spot wild bison, feral horses, prairie dogs, and elk against vivid badland rock layers.
* **Wind Canyon Trail:** A short, easy hike that offers one of the most breathtaking panoramic sunset views over the Little Missouri River.
* **Maltese Cross Cabin:** Located right behind the South Unit Visitor Center in town, this is the original cabin Roosevelt lived in during his time ranching in Dakota Territory.

---

### 2. Attend the *Medora Musical*
A quintessential Medora tradition, this high-energy outdoor show takes place every summer in the **Burning Hills Amphitheatre**. 
* Set against the natural backdrop of the Badlands, it blends Western-style song and dance, humor, live animals, and patriotic history.
* Be sure to book tickets well in advance if visiting between June and early September.

---

### 3. Dine at the Pitchfork Steak Fondue
Located on the bluff overlooking the town right next to the amphitheater, this is the classic pre-show dinner:
* Chefs load 12-ounce strip steaks onto actual pitchforks and plunge them into vats of boiling oil.
* Served buffet-style alongside baked potatoes, baked beans, coleslaw, and brownies, it pairs great food with sprawling badlands views.

---

### 4. Step Back in Time at Chateau de Mòres
Medora was founded in 1883 by a French nobleman, the Marquis de Mòres, who named the town after his wife, Medora von Hoffman.
* **The Chateau:** A 26-room, two-story wooden summer home preserved as a historic site. Many original personal artifacts and furnishings remain untouched.
* **Packing Plant Chimney:** Down in the valley, visit the ruins and brick chimney of the Marquis's ambitious (and ill-fated) refrigerated beef packing enterprise.

---

### 5. Visit the North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame
Located right in the center of town, this state-of-the-art 15,000-square-foot museum celebrates Plains Indian culture, ranching history, and rodeo heritage. It features interactive exhibits, Western art, and historic saddlery and regalia.

---

### 6. Hike or Bike the Maah Daah Hey Trail
For outdoor enthusiasts, the **Maah Daah Hey Trail** is an internationally acclaimed 144-mile non-motorized single-track trail cutting across the Badlands.
* Medora serves as a major hub for the trail.
* Even if you aren't doing a multi-day bikepacking trip, you can hike or mountain bike scenic day-use segments directly accessible from or near town.

---

### 7. Play a Round at Bully Pulpit Golf Course
Ranked among the top public golf courses in the United States, Bully Pulpit winds through meadows, woodlands, and dramatic badlands canyons. The signature holes along the cliffs and gorges (holes 14 through 16) offer spectacular views and an unforgettable challenge.

---

### 8. Stroll Downtown Medora & Point to Point Park
* **Wooden Boardwalks & Shops:** Spend an afternoon wandering past historic storefronts, Western-wear boutiques, the town bakery, and ice cream parlors.
* **Point to Point Park:** A family-friendly complex featuring an 18-hole miniature golf course, a zipline across the badlands, and a pool/lazy river.
* **Little Missouri Saloon:** A great stop for a cold beer, a burger, and authentic rustic saloon vibes.

---

### Tips for Visiting:
* **Seasonality:** Medora is heavily seasonal. Most shops, restaurants, and the *Medora Musical* operate from **late May through mid-September**. While Theodore Roosevelt National Park is open year-round, many town amenities close for the winter.
* **Accommodations:** Historic lodging like the **Rough Riders Hotel** fills up fast, so reserve your room months ahead for summer trips.

This 3-day road trip showcases the best of western North Dakota: rugged badlands, vast prairie skies, vibrant wildlife, folk art, and rich Western history. 

---

### **Trip Overview**
* **Route:** Enchanted Highway $\rightarrow$ Medora (TRNP South Unit) $\rightarrow$ Watford City (TRNP North Unit) $\rightarrow$ Williston (Fort Union)
* **Total Drive Time:** ~6 to 7 hours of driving spread across 3 days.
* **Best Time to Go:** June through September (for warm weather, open trails, and the summer Medora Musical).

---

### **Day 1: Giant Folk Art & Historic Medora**

#### **Morning: The Enchanted Highway**
* **Drive the Highway:** Start just off I-94 at Gladstone and drive south along the **Enchanted Highway** toward Regent (32 miles). This route features some of the world’s largest scrap-metal folk art sculptures, including *Geese in Flight*, *Deer Crossing*, and *Pheasants on the Prairie*.
* **Stop in Regent:** Grab a coffee or homemade pie at the gift shop at the end of the route before heading west toward Medora.

#### **Afternoon: Step Back into the Old West in Medora**
* **Explore Historic Medora:** This charming 1880s cow town was Theodore Roosevelt’s stomping grounds. Walk the wooden boardwalks and visit:
  * **Chateau de Mores State Historic Site:** The 26-room summer home built in 1883 by the eccentric French nobleman who founded Medora.
  * **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame:** A sleek, engaging museum celebrating Native American, rodeo, and ranching heritage.

#### **Evening: Badlands Dinner & A Show**
* **Pitchfork Steak Fondue:** Head up to the bluff overlooking Medora, where chefs plunge 12-oz steaks onto pitchforks and submerge them in boiling vats of oil.
* **The Medora Musical:** Held outdoors at the Burning Hills Amphitheater (nightly June–September), this high-energy musical production celebrates Teddy Roosevelt and Western history against the backdrop of the badlands.

* **Where to Stay:** The historic *Rough Riders Hotel* or a cabin in Medora.

---

### **Day 2: Theodore Roosevelt National Park – South Unit**

#### **Morning: Maltese Cross Cabin & Scenic Loop**
* **Visitor Center & Maltese Cross Cabin:** Start at the South Unit entrance in Medora. Tour Teddy Roosevelt’s actual temporary cabin, which was relocated here and furnished with period pieces (including his writing desk).
* **Scenic Drive:** Drive the paved scenic loop winding through multi-colored badlands formations, bentonite clay buttes, and juniper coulees. 
* **Wildlife Watching:** You are virtually guaranteed to see **bison** herds, sprawling **black-tailed prairie dog towns**, and often **wild/feral horses**.

#### **Afternoon: Easy Hikes & Sweeping Vistas**
* **Wind Canyon Trail:** A short, easy 0.4-mile loop along a ridge carved by prevailing winds, offering the best panoramic view of the Little Missouri River curving through the badlands.
* **Buck Hill:** Drive or walk up to the highest accessible point in the park for a 360-degree vista of the park's interior.
* **Picnic at Peaceful Valley:** Relax by the old historic ranch buildings in the valley bottom.

#### **Late Afternoon / Sunset: Painted Canyon**
* Stop at the **Painted Canyon Overlook and Visitor Center** (accessible directly from I-94 exit 23). The view from the rim here reveals deep crimson, tan, and charcoal layers, which look magnificent in the golden hour before sunset.
* **Evening Drive:** Drive north on US-85 (about 1 hour 15 minutes) to stay overnight in **Watford City**.

---

### **Day 3: Rugged North Unit & Fur Trade History**

#### **Morning: Theodore Roosevelt National Park – North Unit**
* **Why it’s a must-see:** The North Unit is less visited, much more rugged, and features dramatic, deep river canyons.
* **River Bend Overlook:** The signature photo-op of the park. Walk out to the 1930s Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) stone shelter perched high over the Little Missouri River valley.
* **Oxbow Overlook:** Drive to the end of the 14-mile scenic drive to see the dramatic horseshoe bend of the river. 
* **Wildlife:** Keep an eye out for **bighorn sheep** picking their way along the high cliffs, as well as the park's managed herd of **Longhorn cattle**.

#### **Afternoon: Fort Union Trading Post & The Confluence**
* Drive about 1 hour northwest toward the Montana border near Williston:
  * **Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site:** A remarkably detailed, fully reconstructed 1830s–1860s fur trading post. At its peak, Plains tribes (Assiniboine, Mandan, Blackfeet) and European traders met here peacefully to trade buffalo robes for guns, cloth, and glass beads.
  * **Missouri-Yellowstone Confluence Interpretive Center:** Located just minutes away, this center marks where the Missouri and Yellowstone rivers meet—a key landmark documented by Lewis and Clark in 1805.

#### **Evening: Wrap-Up**
* Enjoy dinner in **Williston** (try local steakhouses or craft breweries like *Williston Brewing Company*), where you can catch a flight home from Sloulin Field/Williston Basin Airport (XWA) or loop back east toward Bismarck.

---

### **Essential Road Trip Tips**
1. **America the Beautiful Pass:** Theodore Roosevelt National Park charges an entrance fee ($30/vehicle), but the National Parks Pass is accepted for both the South and North units.
2. **Bison Safety:** Keep at least 25 yards (approx. 2 bus lengths) away from bison. Do not approach them on foot, especially during the mid-summer rut.
3. **Connectivity:** Cell service can be patchy to non-existent between Watford City, the North Unit, and rural stretches along the highway—download offline Google Maps ahead of time.
4. **Time Zones:** Medora and Watford City are in the **Mountain Time Zone**, while eastern North Dakota (Bismarck) is in **Central Time**. Keep this in mind when timing shows and reservations.

The drive from Mount Rushmore (South Dakota) to the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Medora, North Dakota) is relatively short—roughly **240 miles (about 4 to 4.5 hours)** if driving directly via US-85 North. 

Because the direct drive isn't overwhelmingly long, you have plenty of time to add a scenic detour or break up the trip with quirky roadside landmarks, Wild West history, and natural sights.

Here are the best stops along the way, arranged from south to north:

---

### 1. In the Northern Black Hills (First 1–2 hours)
Before leaving South Dakota’s Black Hills region, there are two classic routes:

* **Deadwood, SD:** Just north of Rushmore, this historic gold-rush town is famous for legends like Wild Bill Hickok and Calamity Jane. You can walk the historic Main Street, visit Mount Moriah Cemetery where Hickok and Calamity Jane are buried, or grab lunch.
* **Spearfish Canyon Scenic Byway (US-14A):** If you prefer nature over casinos/history, route through Spearfish Canyon instead of the highway. It’s a 19-mile drive flanked by towering limestone cliffs, ponderosa pines, and easily accessible roadside waterfalls like **Bridal Veil Falls** and **Roughlock Falls**.

---

### 2. The Classic Detour: Devils Tower National Monument (Wyoming)
* **Time addition:** Adds about 1.5 to 2 hours of driving, plus 1–2 hours on site.
* If you have not seen America’s first national monument, this is your best chance. Instead of heading straight north on US-85, take I-90 West into Wyoming, head up to **Devils Tower**, and then cut northeast through Hulett and Aladdin back toward Belle Fourche. 
* Walking the flat, paved **1.3-mile Tower Trail** around the base gives you incredible perspectives of the massive volcanic monolith.

---

### 3. Roadside Curiosities along US-85
Once you leave the Black Hills and head onto US-85 North, the landscape shifts into expansive open prairie and rolling buttes:

* **Center of the Nation Monument (Belle Fourche, SD):** Belle Fourche is the geographic center of the 50 United States (designated after Alaska and Hawaii joined). In town, the **Tri-State Museum** has a giant 21-foot granite compass rose marker that makes for a great photo op. *(The actual, precise survey marker is on a gravel pasture road about 20 miles north, but the museum site is where most people stop).*
* **Slim Buttes / Castles National Natural Landmark:** As you drive north through the Custer National Forest portion of Harding County, keep an eye out for dramatic sandstone cliff formations rising sharply out of the plains.
* **Pioneer Trails Museum (Bowman, ND):** A surprisingly thorough small-town museum featuring an impressive collection of local dinosaur fossils (triceratops, hadrosaurs), regional indigenous artifacts, and pioneer history.
* **White Butte, ND:** For avid "highpointers," North Dakota’s highest natural point (3,506 ft) is located just east of US-85 near Amidon. It’s an easy-to-moderate 1.4-mile round-trip hike with panoramic views across the prairie, though it is on private land with a designated public easement and donation box at the trailhead.

---

### 4. Medora & The Gateway to Theodore Roosevelt NP
You will finish your drive in **Medora**, the historic cowboy town right at the gate of the park's South Unit:

* **Chateau de Mores State Historic Site:** The 26-room summer home built in 1883 by the eccentric French nobleman who founded Medora.
* **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame:** Located right downtown, showcasing Native American, ranching, and rodeo heritage.
* **Pitchfork Steak Fondue & Medora Musical (Summer only):** If visiting between June and early September, this outdoor amphitheater show and cowboy-style dinner overlooking the Badlands is a beloved local tradition.

---

### Road Trip Tips:
1. **Services are sparse:** Once you pass Belle Fourche, towns are few and far between. Fuel up and grab snacks in **Belle Fourche, SD** or **Bowman, ND**.
2. **Which Park Unit?** Medora sits at the entrance to the **South Unit** (the most visited part of TRNP). If you are visiting the rugged and quieter **North Unit** near Watford City, continue north on US-85 for another 70 miles (about 1 hour and 15 minutes past Medora).

Traveling along Interstate 94 through North Dakota is one of the classic American plains road trips. Stretching roughly 350 miles from the Red River in the east to the badlands in the west, here are the best stops along the route, ordered from **East to West**:

---

### 1. Fargo (Milepost 345–352)
North Dakota’s largest city offers a vibrant downtown, arts, and quirky pop culture:
* **The Famous Woodchipper:** Stop by the Fargo-Moorhead Visitors Center to take a photo with the actual prop woodchipper from the Coen brothers’ movie *Fargo*.
* **Fargo Air Museum:** Features historic, flyable aircraft from WWII through the modern era.
* **Bonanzaville, USA (West Fargo):** A 12-acre pioneer village with dozens of preserved historic buildings, antique farm equipment, and prairie artifacts.

---

### 2. Valley City: "The City of Bridges" (Exit 292)
Nestled in the lush Sheyenne River Valley, Valley City is known for its historic bridges and scenic river views:

---

### 3. Jamestown: The Buffalo City (Exit 256–258)
Jamestown is the quintessential prairie roadside stop:

* **Frontier Village:** A replica pioneer town located beside the museum, featuring the original writer's shack of western novelist Louis L'Amour.

---

### 4. Iconic Roadside Giants: Steele & New Salem
If you enjoy massive roadside sculptures, watch for these two exits:
* **Sandy the Sandhill Crane (Steele, Exit 200):** At 40 feet tall, it's the world’s largest sandhill crane.
* **Salem Sue (New Salem, Exit 127):** Perched high on School Hill overlooking I-94, this 38-foot-tall fiberglass Holstein cow honors local dairy farmers and offers a commanding 360-degree panoramic view of the prairie.

---

### 5. Bismarck & Mandan (Exits 156–159)
The state capital sits on the Missouri River and offers some of the state's richest history:
* **North Dakota Heritage Center & State Museum:** Located on the Capitol grounds, this world-class, free museum covers everything from dinosaur fossils found in the state to Native American culture and space exploration.

---

### 6. The Enchanted Highway (Gladstone, Exit 72)
* At Exit 72, you'll immediately see **"Geese in Flight,"** officially recognized by Guinness World Records as the world’s largest scrap metal sculpture. 
* If you have an hour to spare, you can drive 32 miles south along a paved country road to Regent, passing six more enormous metal folk-art sculptures (including giant grasshoppers, pheasants, and a tin family).

---

### 7. Dickinson (Exits 59–64)
* **Badlands Dinosaur Museum:** Located at the Dickinson Museum Center, this is a must-stop for fossil enthusiasts, housing thousands of rare dinosaur bones and fossil specimens unearthed in the surrounding region.
* **Ukrainian Cultural Institute:** Highlights the heritage of the Ukrainian immigrants who settled in southwestern North Dakota.

---

### 8. Painted Canyon Overlook (Exit 32)
* **The Best Rest Stop on I-94:** Even if you aren't planning a long hike, do not miss the **Painted Canyon Visitor Center**. Directly off the highway, you can step out of your car and look over the canyon rim into the layered, multicolored badlands. Wild bison often graze near the parking lot.

### 9. Medora & Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Exit 24 & 27)
The crown jewel of North Dakota travel sits right at the western end of the state:

While all 15 official National Archives (NARA) presidential libraries offer rich archives for researchers, several stand out above the rest for general visitors due to their dramatic exhibits, iconic artifacts, architecture, and beautiful settings. 

The top presidential libraries most widely considered worth a visit include:

---

### 1. Ronald Reagan Presidential Library & Museum (Simi Valley, California)
* **The Vibe:** Sweeping, dramatic, and crowd-pleasing.
* **Why it’s worth visiting:** Perched high on a hill with panoramic views of Southern California, it feels almost like a presidential theme park. 
* **Standout features:** 
  * The centerpiece is the **Air Force One Pavilion**, where you can step inside the actual Boeing 707 used by Reagan (and six other presidents).
  * A full-scale replica of the Oval Office.
  * An authentic, full-size segment of the Berlin Wall.
  * Reagan’s Marine One helicopter and secret service motorcade vehicles.

### 2. Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum (Hyde Park, New York)
* **The Vibe:** Deeply historical, serene, and iconic.
* **Why it’s worth visiting:** FDR essentially invented the modern presidential library. Located in New York’s scenic Hudson River Valley, it covers two of the most pivotal eras in modern history: the Great Depression and World War II.
* **Standout features:** 
  * You can tour **Springwood** (FDR’s lifelong home), Eleanor Roosevelt’s retreat at **Val-Kill**, and his private getaway, **Top Cottage**.
  * The museum features FDR’s specially modified Ford convertible with hand controls, his Fireside Chat microphones, and candid exhibits on the New Deal and the Manhattan Project.

### 3. Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum (Springfield, Illinois)
* **The Vibe:** Immersive, theatrical, and emotionally powerful.
* **Note:** This is run by the State of Illinois rather than the National Archives, but it is routinely ranked among the very best presidential museums in the country.
* **Why it’s worth visiting:** It uses high-production theater techniques, life-sized hyper-realistic wax figures, and holographic presentations to bring the 1860s and the Civil War to life.
* **Standout features:** 
  * Life-size walk-throughs of Lincoln’s boyhood cabin and the 1861 White House.
  * Rare artifacts, including the Gettysburg Address, Lincoln’s stovepipe hat, and the quill pen used to sign the Emancipation Proclamation.
  * Lincoln’s home and his tomb are both just a short drive away in Springfield.

### 4. John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum (Boston, Massachusetts)
* **The Vibe:** Striking architecture, mid-century elegance, and nostalgic idealism.
* **Why it’s worth visiting:** Designed by famed architect **I.M. Pei**, the building itself is a masterpiece of glass, steel, and concrete sitting right on the water overlooking Boston Harbor.
* **Standout features:** 
  * Exhibits dedicated to the 1960 televised debates, the Space Race, the Cuban Missile Crisis, and Jackie Kennedy’s fashion and White House restoration.
  * A 115-foot glass pavilion offering floor-to-ceiling views of the water, intentionally designed as a quiet, reflective space to end the tour.

### 5. Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library (Austin, Texas)
* **The Vibe:** Monumental, candid, and politically fascinating.
* **Why it’s worth visiting:** Located on the University of Texas campus, this massive 10-story monolith doesn’t shy away from the contradictions of LBJ’s presidency—balancing the triumphs of the Civil Rights movement and Great Society against the devastation of the Vietnam War.
* **Standout features:** 
  * The **Great Hall**, where four floors of red-buckram archive boxes containing over 45 million documents are visible behind a four-story glass wall.
  * Interactive telephones where you can listen to LBJ’s actual, unvarnished White House telephone recordings (famous for his blunt, colorful phone presence).
  * *Tip:* Pair it with a drive out to Johnson City to tour the **LBJ Ranch** (the "Texas White House").

### 6. Harry S. Truman Presidential Library and Museum (Independence, Missouri)
* **The Vibe:** Thought-provoking, modern, and high-impact.
* **Why it’s worth visiting:** Fresh off a massive $30+ million renovation, Truman’s library was completely reimagined to tell the story of a sudden president faced with monumental world-altering decisions.
* **Standout features:** 
  * Highly interactive exhibits that put you in Truman's shoes during the decision to drop the atomic bomb, the creation of the United Nations, and the start of the Cold War.
  * Truman’s office kept exactly as it was when he worked there after his presidency, alongside the courtyard where he and Bess are buried.

---

### Honorable Mentions:
* **George W. Bush (Dallas, TX):** Features a poignant 9/11 exhibit containing a massive piece of mangled World Trade Center steel, plus an interactive "Decision Points Theater."
* **Dwight D. Eisenhower (Abilene, KS):** Completely updated in 2019; essential for WWII buffs, featuring his boyhood home and grave site.
* **Jimmy Carter (Atlanta, GA):** Focuses heavily on human rights, peace negotiations (Camp David Accords), and his post-presidential global humanitarian work, all set in peaceful Japanese gardens.

### Tips for Visiting:
* **Pair with historic homes:** The best visits (FDR, Lincoln, Truman, Eisenhower, LBJ) allow you to tour the president's actual home alongside the library.
* **Time commitment:** Budget **2.5 to 4 hours** per library; places like Reagan or FDR can easily take half a day or more if you walk the grounds.

---

### 1. In-Person Destinations in North Dakota

* **Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Medora & Watford City, ND)**
  * **Maltese Cross Cabin (South Unit Visitor Center):** Located right behind the South Unit visitor center in Medora, this is the restored temporary cabin Roosevelt lived in when he first invested in cattle in 1883. It contains period furnishings, including his writing desk and traveling trunk.
  * **Elkhorn Ranch Unit:** Known as TR’s "home ranch" and sanctuary following the sudden deaths of his wife and mother in 1884. Located 35 miles north of Medora along the Little Missouri River, it is preserved in its wild, remote state. While the timber cabin is gone, the stone foundations remain, and interpretive markers detail how he lived and wrote there.
  * **North and South Units:** Driving the scenic loops and hiking the backcountry trails lets you see the bison, feral horses, and rugged terrain that forged his lifelong commitment to conservation.

* **The Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library (Medora, ND)**
  * Located on a bluff overlooking Medora and the Badlands, this museum and cultural center explores Roosevelt’s life with a heavy emphasis on his time in Dakota Territory, his conservation legacy, and the ecology of the American West.

* **The Historic Town of Medora**
  * **Chateau de Mores State Historic Site:** The summer home of Antoine de Vallombrosa, the Marquis de Mores—a French nobleman and rival/contemporary of Roosevelt who founded Medora in 1883. Visiting the chateau offers vital context on the 1880s cattle boom that drew Roosevelt to the territory.
  * **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame:** Located in Medora, this museum details the open-range cattle era, regional Native American history, and ranching culture of TR’s era.

---

### 2. Digital & Academic Archives

* **The Theodore Roosevelt Center at Dickinson State University (Dickinson, ND)**
  * Located roughly 35 miles east of Medora, the TR Center maintains a comprehensive, searchable digital archive of Roosevelt's papers.
  * It includes digitized personal letters, ranching ledgers, diary entries, and photographs documenting his day-to-day life as a Dakota cattleman. Many of these primary sources are accessible free online at [TheodoreRooseveltCenter.org](https://www.theodorerooseveltcenter.org/).

---

### 3. Recommended Reading & Roosevelt’s Own Words

* ***Ranch Life and the Hunting-Trail* (1888) by Theodore Roosevelt:** TR’s firsthand account of his years in the Badlands, featuring original illustrations by Frederic Remington.
* ***Hunting Trips of a Ranchman* (1885) by Theodore Roosevelt:** Written from his Maltese Cross cabin, chronicling his early days tracking game across western Dakota.
* ***Theodore Roosevelt in the Badlands: A Young Politician's Quest for Recovery in the American West* by Clay S. Jenkinson:** A detailed historical examination focused exclusively on how the territory reshaped Roosevelt’s identity, health, and politics.
* ***The Rise of Theodore Roosevelt* by Edmund Morris:** The first volume of Morris’s acclaimed biography features extensive chapters on TR’s grief, ranching adventures, and famous pursuit of boat thieves down the Little Missouri River.

Theodore Roosevelt’s life as a rancher, naturalist, soldier, and president is memorialized across several national historic sites, parks, and landmarks. The most significant historic sites connected to him include:

---

### **1. Official Homes & Presidential Sites**

* **Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site (New York, NY)**
  * **Significance:** Roosevelt was born here on October 27, 1858, and lived in this brownstone until he was 14. The original building was demolished in 1916, but following his death in 1919, the Women’s Theodore Roosevelt Memorial Association rebuilt an exact replica, furnished with many original family heirlooms.

* **Sagamore Hill National Historic Site (Oyster Bay, Long Island, NY)**
  * **Significance:** Known as Roosevelt’s primary family home from 1885 until his death in 1919, it served as his **"Summer White House"** during his presidency (1902–1908). The site contains the original 23-room Queen Anne-style home filled with hunting trophies, books, and memorabilia, as well as the Old Orchard Museum and the surrounding nature trails. Roosevelt is buried nearby at **Youngs Memorial Cemetery**.

* **Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site (Ansley Wilcox House – Buffalo, NY)**
  * **Significance:** Following the assassination of President William McKinley at the Pan-American Exposition in September 1901, Vice President Roosevelt rushed to Buffalo and took the presidential oath of office in the library of this Greek Revival mansion, officially becoming the 26th U.S. president.

* **Pine Knot (Albemarle County, near Keene, VA)**
  * **Significance:** A modest, rustic two-story cottage purchased by Edith and Theodore Roosevelt in 1905 to serve as a secret weekend getaway and birdwatching retreat during his presidency. It is preserved today by the Edith and Theodore Roosevelt Pine Knot Foundation.

---

### **2. The Badlands & The Frontier**

* **Theodore Roosevelt National Park (North Dakota)**
  * **Significance:** In 1883, Roosevelt went to the Dakota Badlands to hunt bison and grieve the tragic, same-day deaths of his wife, Alice, and mother, Mittie, in 1884. His time as a cattle rancher shaped his philosophy on conservation and resilience. 
  * Key sites within the park include:
    * **Maltese Cross Cabin:** His first ranch home, which was relocated and restored at the South Unit visitor center.
    * **Elkhorn Ranch Site:** His secluded "home ranch" along the Little Missouri River, which he considered his true sanctuary.

---

### **3. Military & "Rough Riders" Landmarks**

* **The Menger Hotel (San Antonio, TX)**
  * **Significance:** During the Spanish-American War in 1898, Roosevelt used the Menger Hotel’s Victorian bar to recruit members for the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry—better known as the **Rough Riders**. The historic bar is still preserved with Rough Rider memorabilia and bullet holes reputedly fired during the recruitment era.

* **Tampa Bay Hotel (Now the Henry B. Plant Museum – Tampa, FL)**
  * **Significance:** Before embarking for Cuba in 1898, Roosevelt and top military officers made this Gilded Age hotel their official headquarters and staging base.

---

### **4. Major Memorials**

* **Theodore Roosevelt Island (Washington, D.C.)**
  * **Significance:** An 88.5-acre wooded island in the Potomac River administered by the National Park Service. It serves as a living memorial honoring his conservation legacy, centered around a 17-foot bronze statue of Roosevelt and inscribed granite monoliths featuring his quotes on nature and civic duty.

* **Mount Rushmore National Memorial (Keystone, SD)**
  * **Significance:** Roosevelt’s 60-foot likeness is carved into the granite face alongside George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and Abraham Lincoln. Sculptor Gutzon Borglum chose Roosevelt to represent the growth, economic development, and global emergence of the United States in the 20th century.

Located in **Medora, North Dakota**—perched on a butte just outside the entrance to Theodore Roosevelt National Park—the institution offers an experience distinctly different from traditional presidential libraries. 

Here is a breakdown of what makes it stand out and practical considerations to weigh before planning a trip:

---

### Why It’s Worth Visiting

* **A Striking Architectural & Environmental Feat:**  
  Designed by the world-renowned architecture firm **Snøhetta**, the building is engineered to blend seamlessly into the dramatic Badlands landscape. Built to meet the stringent criteria of the **Living Building Challenge**, it is designed to be self-sustaining (net-zero energy and water). It features walkable, green rooftops, outdoor native prairie boardwalks, and sweeping 360-degree views over the rugged buttes.

* **An Immersive, Modern Museum (Not a Dusty Archive):**  
  Because Roosevelt’s presidential papers are housed at the Library of Congress, the Medora facility was built as an experiential, multimedia museum. Its Narrative and Adventure Galleries take visitors chronologically from his frail childhood in New York to his transformative ranching years in the Badlands, the Rough Riders, and his conservation-defining presidency. Interactive features (such as personalized digital visitor profiles) make the history engaging for adults and younger visitors alike.

* **Place-Based Historical Significance:**  
  Roosevelt famously stated, *“I never would have been President if it had not been for my experiences in North Dakota.”* Unlike presidential libraries placed simply in a president's birthplace or suburban home, this library sits directly on the rugged landscape that shaped Roosevelt's character and his philosophy on public lands and wildlife conservation.

* **Ideal Pairing with Theodore Roosevelt National Park:**  
  The library serves as a natural cultural and educational gateway to **Theodore Roosevelt National Park** (South Unit). You can easily pair museum exploration with hiking, scenic loop drives, and spotting wild horses, bison, and prairie dog colonies.

---

### Considerations & Drawbacks

* **Remote Location:**  
  Medora is isolated. It sits on Interstate 94 roughly 2 hours west of Bismarck, ND, and about 4 hours from Billings, Montana, or Rapid City, South Dakota. Unless you are already on a cross-country or national parks road trip, reaching it requires significant travel time.
* **Timed-Entry Tickets:**  
  General admission operates on a timed-entry reservation system to manage crowd flow; booking tickets ahead of time via their website is recommended during peak travel months.
* **Seasonal Shifts:**  
  Medora thrives as a lively summer destination (featuring the outdoor *Medora Musical* and pitchfork steak fondues), but during late fall, winter, and early spring, temperatures drop sharply, and hours across town and the library are more limited.

### The Bottom Line
If you are expecting a traditional, paper-focused presidential archive, this isn't it. But if you want a **state-of-the-art storytelling museum celebrating conservation, resilience, and history**, integrated into one of the most scenic national park backdrops in the country, it is well worth adding to your travel bucket list.

Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th President of the United States (1901–1909), was a transformative figure who redefined the American presidency. Taking office at age 42 following William McKinley’s assassination, he remains the youngest person to ever become president. His presidency was marked by boundless energy, progressive reform, and bold foreign policy.

---

### 1. Major Accomplishments

Roosevelt governed under a domestic agenda known as the **"Square Deal,"** designed to ensure fair treatment for capital, labor, and the public.

#### Domestic Policy & Progressive Reforms
* **"Trust-Busting" and Corporate Regulation:** 
  Roosevelt believed large corporations should serve the public good. He directed the Department of Justice to enforce the previously underused Sherman Antitrust Act, breaking up monopolistic combinations such as J.P. Morgan’s Northern Securities Company (railroads), the Beef Trust, and Standard Oil. He filed 44 antitrust suits, earning the moniker "the Trust Buster" (though he distinguished between "bad trusts" that abused their monopoly power and "good trusts" that operated efficiently).
* **Consumer Protection:** 
  Spurred by Upton Sinclair’s exposé *The Jungle*, Roosevelt pushed through landmark consumer protection legislation in 1906:
  * **Meat Inspection Act:** Mandated sanitary standards and federal inspection of livestock and slaughterhouses.
  * **Pure Food and Drug Act:** Banned mislabeled or adulterated foods and drugs, paving the way for the modern Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
* **Railroad Regulation:** 
  He strengthened the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) through the **Elkins Act (1903)**, which penalized rail rebates, and the **Hepburn Act (1906)**, which gave the ICC the power to set maximum railroad rates.
* **Labor Mediation:** 
  During the **1902 Anthracite Coal Strike**, Roosevelt broke precedent by refusing to automatically side with corporate owners. Instead, he summoned both labor leaders and mine owners to the White House to arbitrate, threatening to send federal troops to run the mines if owners refused to negotiate. This was the first time a president acted as an impartial mediator in a labor dispute.

#### Foreign Policy: "Speak Softly and Carry a Big Stick"
* **The Panama Canal:** 
  Determined to connect the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, Roosevelt supported Panamanian separatists in breaking away from Colombia in 1903. Once Panama declared independence, the U.S. secured rights to the Canal Zone and began construction on the engineering marvel, which opened in 1914.
* **The Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (1904):** 
  Roosevelt declared that the U.S. had the right to intervene as an "international police power" in Latin American nations to prevent European intervention and financial instability.
* **Nobel Peace Prize (1906):** 
  He mediated an end to the Russo-Japanese War, hosting negotiations in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. For orchestrating the Treaty of Portsmouth, he became the first American to win a Nobel Prize.
* **The Great White Fleet (1907–1909):** 
  To showcase the burgeoning power of the modernized U.S. Navy and deter foreign aggression, Roosevelt sent 16 gleaming battleships on a 14-month circumnavigation of the globe.

---

### 2. Conservation Work

Roosevelt considered conservation his most enduring contribution, earning him the title of the **"Conservationist President."** Influenced by wilderness icons like John Muir and his first Chief of the U.S. Forest Service, Gifford Pinchot, Roosevelt rejected the era's unregulated exploitation of natural resources in favor of sustainable, scientific management and preservation.

During his presidency, Roosevelt protected approximately **230 million acres** of public land. His key conservation achievements include:

* **The Antiquities Act of 1906:** 
  One of the most significant pieces of conservation legislation in U.S. history, this act empowered presidents to bypass Congress to unilaterally designate federal lands of historic or scientific interest as National Monuments. Roosevelt immediately used it to protect **Devils Tower** (the first), and later the **Grand Canyon**, **Muir Woods**, and **Mount Olympus**.
* **U.S. Forest Service (1905):** 
  He created the United States Forest Service under the Department of Agriculture, placing Gifford Pinchot at the helm to manage timberlands for long-term sustainability rather than short-term profit.
* **Establishment of Public Lands:**
  * **5 National Parks:** Crater Lake, Wind Cave, Sullys Hill (later a game preserve), Mesa Verde, and Platt.
  * **18 National Monuments:** Including the Grand Canyon and Petrified Forest (both later upgraded to National Parks).
  * **51 Federal Bird Reserves:** Starting with **Pelican Island, Florida (1903)**, which established the foundation for today’s National Wildlife Refuge System.
  * **150 National Forests** and **4 National Game Preserves**.
* **Newlands Reclamation Act (1902):** 
  Funded irrigation projects across 20 arid Western states, opening millions of acres to settlement and agriculture.

---

### 3. Legacy

Roosevelt’s presidency left an indelible mark on American institutions, politics, and culture:

* **Creation of the Modern Presidency:** 
  Before Roosevelt, Congress dominated 19th-century American politics. Roosevelt dramatically expanded executive power, viewing the presidency as a **"bully pulpit"**—a platform to advocate for moral causes, mobilize public opinion, and actively guide legislation. Every activist president since has operated in the model he created.
* **Precursor to Modern Progressivism:** 
  His Square Deal and later 1912 "New Nationalism" campaign (with the Progressive/Bull Moose Party) laid the conceptual foundation for future federal social safety nets, including Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal and Lyndon B. Johnson's Great Society.
